questions.subtopic: 4C3 Planning around key risks and controls. Fraud for the organization's benefit
questions.question: A sales director at a Thai machinery maker bribes a customer's buyer to win an order and books the payment as marketing, gaining nothing personally. How should internal auditor Niran BEST classify the act?

options.A: As fraud committed to gain an unlawful business advantage
options.B: As a commercial decision outside the meaning of fraud
options.C: As a recording error in the marketing expense account
options.D: As a conflict of interest held by the sales director

questions.key_concept: Fraud can be committed for the organization as well as against it: the advantage sought may be personal or for the business.
questions.pre_read: Notice who benefits from the act, then ask whether the meaning of fraud depends on who benefits.
questions.correct_explanation: The Standards' glossary treats fraud as a deliberate, deceptive act by a person or an organization to win an unfair or unlawful advantage, and that advantage can be personal or for the business. A hidden bribe booked as marketing fits. Calling it a commercial decision is the runner-up, but benefit to the company does not take an act out of the meaning of fraud.

wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: the company gains, yet the glossary's meaning of fraud covers an unlawful advantage for the business as well as for a person.
wrong_explanations.C: An error is unintended. The director chose to pay the buyer and to disguise the payment, so the wrong account is concealment, not a slip.
wrong_explanations.D: A conflict of interest needs a competing personal interest. The director gains nothing personally; the deception is what matters here.

tips: Eliminate: C, because the mislabeled entry was deliberate, and D, because the director has no competing personal interest in the order.
Final two: A beats B because the meaning of fraud covers an unlawful advantage for the organization, not only personal gain.
Exam cue: fraud can be committed for the organization as well as against it; who benefits does not decide the label.

questions.subtopic: 4C3 Planning around key risks and controls. Fraud risk where no money moves
questions.question: Internal auditor Katrin is planning an engagement on safety inspection records at an Icelandic airline maintenance unit that pays bonuses for fast turnaround and handles no money. Which fraud risk should Katrin MOST clearly recognize?

options.A: No fraud risk worth recording in a unit without cash
options.B: Purchasing fraud in the airline's separate spare-parts department
options.C: Inspection sign-offs falsified to protect turnaround bonuses
options.D: Honest recording mistakes made under turnaround pressure

questions.key_concept: Fraud risk is not limited to cash and assets: information can be falsified on purpose to gain an unfair advantage.
questions.pre_read: Ask what could be deliberately falsified in this activity, and who would gain from it.
questions.correct_explanation: Fraud is any deliberate deception for an unfair advantage, and the glossary's description names forgery and misuse of information as well as assets. A bonus tied to speed gives staff a reason to sign off inspections that were not done. Standard 13.2 requires fraud risk to be considered in every engagement. Looking at purchasing is the runner-up, but it follows the money and misses the records under review.

wrong_explanations.A: Fraud does not need cash. The glossary's description covers deceit, forgery and misuse of information for an unfair advantage, such as a bonus.
wrong_explanations.B: Closest choice: purchasing does carry fraud risk, but it is another department's activity. The records under review can themselves be falsified for gain.
wrong_explanations.D: A mistake made under turnaround pressure is an error, because nothing is intended. The question asks for a fraud risk, which needs a deliberate act.

tips: Eliminate: A, because fraud covers falsified information as well as stolen assets, and D, because an honest mistake has no intent.
Final two: C beats B because the fraud risk to weigh sits in the activity under review; falsified records can earn a bonus without any cash moving.
Exam cue: when a process handles no money, ask what information could be falsified and who would gain from it.
